Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . rewritten: The European lobster, scientifically referred to as Homarus gammarus, is an Atlantic Ocean inhabitant, including the Mediterranean and certain regions within the Black Sea. It's closely related to the American lobster (H. americanus). Capable of growing up to 60 cm (24 inches) in length and reaching a weight of 6 kg (13 lbs), it's identifiable by its prominent pair of claws. While they're blue when alive, they turn "lobster red" upon cooking. Reproduction occurs during summer, resulting in the female carrying eggs for about a year before they hatch into larvae. Esteemed for culinary purposes, Homarus gammarus is extensively caught through lobster pots, primarily around the British Isles.

Homarus gammarus, a sizable crustacean species, can grow up to 60 centimeters (24 inches) in length and weigh between 5-6 kilograms (11-13 pounds). However, lobsters captured using lobster pots typically measure around 23-38 centimeters (9-15 inches) in length and weigh approximately 0.7-2.2 kilograms (1.5-4.9 pounds). Similar to other crustaceans, lobsters possess a rigid exoskeleton that they need to molt, or shed, in order to expand; a process known as ecdysis. Younger lobsters might molt several times annually, whereas older individuals might undergo molting only once every 1-2 years.

The initial duo of pereiopods feature a sizable, uneven pair of claws. The predominant one is referred to as the 'crusher', distinguished by its rounded nodules that facilitate the process of crushing prey; conversely, the secondary claw, known as the 'cutter', is equipped with sharp inner edges, primarily utilized for either gripping or severing the prey. Typically, the left claw serves as the crusher, while the right claw takes on the role of the cutter.

In its natural state, the exoskeleton primarily appears blue on the top surface, featuring amalgamating spots, while the underside reveals a yellow hue. An interesting transformation takes place with the addition of red coloring to lobsters post-cooking. This alteration originates from the fact that during the living phase, a pigment called astaxanthin is intricately linked to a protein complex within their bodies. Upon exposure to heat during the cooking process, this complex disintegrates, leading to the liberation of the red pigment and consequently, the emergence of the red coloration typically associated with lobsters.

The nearest relative of Hermit Crab, Hemithelodus gammarus, is the American Lobster, Homarus americanus. Both species display remarkable likeness and can indeed be interbred under controlled conditions; however, natural hybridization is improbable as their geographical territories do not intersect. Distinctions between these two species can be made through several distinguishing traits.

Female H. gammarus attain sexual maturity once they've reached a carapace length of 80 to 85 millimeters, corresponding to approximately 3 to 3 1/3 inches, with males maturing at a marginally smaller size. Reproduction usually takes place during summer, involving a soft-shelled female who has recently molted, mating with a male having a harder exoskeleton. The female bears the eggs for up to a year, the duration varying based on environmental temperature, adhering them to her pleopods. It is referred to as "berrying" when females carry eggs, and they can be observed at any time of the year.

After hatching during the night, the larvae migrate to the water surface, drifting with ocean currents while they feed on zooplankton. This larval stage, marked by three molts, lasts approximately 15 to 35 days. Post-third molt, the juvenile assumes an appearance more akin to the adult and shifts towards a benthic lifestyle. Juveniles are seldom observed in the wild and have limited documentation, despite their capability for extensive burrowing. Survival rates to the benthic phase are estimated to be exceedingly low - only 1 larva out of 20,000 makes it through. Upon reaching a carapace length of 15 mm (0.59 inches), the juveniles exit their burrows, marking the beginning of their adult life cycle.

Homarus gammarus inhabits the north-eastern Atlantic, ranging from northern Norway through the Azores and Morocco, excluding the Baltic Sea. This species is also prevalent throughout most of the Mediterranean Sea, with the exception being the eastern section beyond Crete, and only parts of the north-western coast of the Black Sea. Among the northernmost occurrences, populations are noted in the Norwegian fjords, notably within the Arctic Circle.

The species comprises four genetically isolated groups: a broad, dispersed population and three specialized entities characterized by limited effective population sizes, potentially linked to adaptation to localized environments. The first group refers to the Norwegian lobster population, often termed the "midnight sun lobster," which stands apart from others. The Mediterranean and Atlantic populations exhibit distinct characteristics. Lastly, there's a Dutch-specific population, evident through samples gathered in the area that differentiated notably from those taken from the North Sea or the English Channel.

Efforts were undertaken to import H. gammarus to New Zealand, along with other European species including the edible crab, Cancer pagurus. In the period between 1904 and 1914, one million lobster juveniles were introduced through hatcheries located in Dunedin. However, this species failed to become established in the area.

In terms of habitat, adult H. gammarus are typically found on the continental shelf within the range of 0 to 150 meters (0-492 ft) in depth. However, their usual depth does not exceed 50 meters (160 ft). These creatures favor hard surfaces like rocks or firm mud, residing in burrows or cracks. During nighttime, they venture out to feed.

Homarus gammarus is vulnerable to a condition referred to as 'unk', which is brought about by the bacterium '<unk>'. This ailment is commonly identified in American lobsters, but its manifestation has been exclusively observed in captive instances of Homarus gammarus. The possibility that the tanks were previously inhabited by Homarus americanus cannot be conclusively dismissed, suggesting a potential source for the disease transmission in these captive environments.

Homarus gammarus, long cherished for its culinary value, notably featured in the 17th-century English folk song "The <unk>", is known for commanding premium prices. Available fresh, frozen, canned, or powdered, it boasts "excellent" white meat from both its claws and abdomen. Virtually all parts of the cephalothorax are edible, with exclusions being the gastric mill and the "sand vein" (gut). Pricing for H. gammarus stands at up to three times the cost of H. americanus; consequently, the European species is prized for its superior flavor profile.

Lobsters are primarily harvested through lobster traps, although occasionally, they might be enticed using lines adorned with octopuses or cuttlefish, thereby making them accessible for capture via netting or manual methods. In 2008, across Europe and North Africa, a total of 4,386 tons of H. gammarus were collected, with a substantial 3,462 tons (accounting for 79%) being sourced from the British Isles, including the Channel Islands. The smallest legal size for landing H. gammarus is specified at a carapace length of 87 mm (approximately 3.4 inches).

H. gammarus, identified as the prototypical species of the Homarus genus by the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature's Direction 51, was previously muddled due to its designation under multiple names like Astacus marinus (Fabricius, 1775) and Homarus vulgaris (H. Milne-Edwards, 1837). This ambiguity compounded when Friedrich Weber's genus description was overlooked until it was later found by Mary Rathbun. Consequently, any preceding attempts to assign a type species for Homarus (H. Milne-Edwards, 1837) became invalid for Homarus Weber, 1795, owing to the rediscovery of Weber's work.

In 1974, L. P. C. Holthuis designated the lectotype for the species Homarus gammarus. This particular specimen was collected at coordinates 57°53′N 11°32′E, located in the vicinity of Marstrand, Sweden (approximately 48 kilometers or 30 miles northwest of Gothenburg). However, both the lectotype and the original specimen have since been misplaced.

Born on July 15, 1914, in Launceston, Tasmania, Frank Headlam was the offspring of agriculturalists Malcolm and Hilda Headlam. Educated at an unspecified college in Hobart, he graduated in 1932. Despite his parents' objections, Headlam enlisted as an air cadet in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) on January 16, 1934. His initial training in aviation took place at the No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) in RAAF Point Cook, Victoria. Consequently, he was promoted to pilot officer upon receiving his commission on January 1, 1935.

Upon finishing his conversion training, Headlam was stationed at Point Cook within the Seaplane Squadron. This small unit, as detailed in the pre-war RAAF's official history, was subordinated to No. 1 Flying Training School. It operated a variety of aircraft, including Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes. While serving there, Headlam was advanced to the rank of flying officer on July 1, 1935. He authored a paper on national defense where he posited that Australia could achieve substantial invulnerability through the deployment of robust air forces, naval assets, including submarines, and static defenses. As noted by Air Force historian Alan Stephens, this paper essentially outlined the 'anti-invasion' idea, which has remained a cornerstone of RAAF strategic thought.

Headlam finished his flying instructor's course in July 1936 and then joined the faculty of the No. 1 Flying Training School. On 1st March 1937, he was promoted to Flight Lieutenant. Starting in July 1938, he participated as one of six students in the Royal Australian Air Force's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course, conducted by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook. This course featured extensive training flights that garnered significant media attention, such as a twelve-day, 10,800 km (6,700 mi) round-Australia voyage by three Avro Ansons in November, with Headlam piloting one of them. In December, he led the Ansons on a six-day往返 journey across Central Australia. Following this, Headlam successfully completed the navigation course with an exceptional distinction. On 27th January 1939, he was transferred to RAAF Station Laverton, Victoria, as a flight commander. Initially serving with No. 2 Squadron, he later moved to No. 1 Squadron on 29th August. Both units operated Avro Ansons.

Upon the commencement of World War II, No. 1 Squadron was primarily involved in escorting convoys and conducting maritime reconnaissance operations along the southern-eastern coast of Australia. Headlam maintained his role within the squadron as a flight commander until the 15th of January, 1940, at which point he transferred to Headquarters Laverton to assume the position of station navigation officer. On the 27th of March, he was then relocated to the staff of the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) headquarters in Melbourne. He received a promotion to squadron leader on the 1st of June, 1940. Exactly two weeks after this promotion, on the 16th of June, he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul's Anglican Church in Frankston; together they had one son and a daughter.

Headlam assumed the leadership of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on April 15, 1941, and was promoted to wing commander on July 1. With Lockheed Hudsons under their command, the squadron primarily carried out maritime patrol missions in southern waters until December 5, when four of their aircraft were dispatched to Darwin, Northern Territory, due to concerns about Japanese military expansion in the Pacific region. On December 7, the detachment set up at Penfui, close to Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the squadron's remaining eight Hudsons remained at Darwin as a reserve. Recognizing that Australia was now engaged in conflict in the Pacific on the following day, one of the Penfui-based Hudsons attacked the suspected radio ship, Nanyo Maru, which was later grounded. By December 12, Headlam had moved to Penfui, taking charge not only as the base commander but also as the leader of No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, dispersing No. 2 Squadron's aircraft at locations including Penfui, an unknown island, and Darwin, enabled attacks on Japanese shipping involved in the invasion of Celebes. Notably, two Hudsons from this detachment successfully engaged enemy floatplanes on 11 January, resulting in the downing or damage of three planes. However, both Hudsons met a similar fate the following day, being shot down by Mitsubishi Zeros. Penfui experienced its initial bombing by the Japanese on 26 January 1942, with subsequent regular attacks causing damage to some aircraft. The surviving Hudsons were subsequently withdrawn to Darwin, while Headlam and his staff stayed behind to ensure the base's readiness for reconnaissance missions from Australia. On 18 February, Headlam received an order to evacuate most of his team, retaining only a small contingent to dismantle the airfield with support from Sparrow Force. Upon returning to Darwin the next day, he witnessed the city's first Japanese raid, which resulted in the destruction of four of No. 2 Squadron's Hudsons. The remaining aircraft were then moved to Daly Waters, where they continued their missions of reconnaissance and bombing against Japanese targets in Timor.

Headlam stayed in Darwin, serving as the Controller of Operations at Headquarters North-Western Area Command until May 12, 1942. Following this, he was transferred to Nhill, Victoria, and became the commanding officer of the No. 2 Air Navigation School, which operated Anson aircraft. In June 1943, the No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron was established with the personnel from this school. On July 20, 1943, Headlam assumed control of the No. 2 Air Observer School (location unspecified), also utilizing Anson aircraft, at Mount Gambier, South Australia. He was later assigned as the senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command on January 12, 1945.

In January 1946, Headlam assumed the role of Officer Commanding for the North-Western Area. By the end of the year, he relocated to Britain and enrolled at the Royal Air Force Staff College in Andover. Thereafter, he served at RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. Upon returning to Australia in November 1947, he took up the position of Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. In November 1950, he succeeded Group Captain Paddy Heffernan as the head of No. 90 (Composite) Wing, which was stationed in Singapore under the command of RAF Changi. This wing oversaw RAAF units operating in the Malayan Emergency, including No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron, which utilized Avro Lincolns for bombings and strikes, and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron, which managed courier services, VIP transportation, and medical evacuations throughout Southeast Asia, as well as troop and cargo airlifts, supply drops to allied forces, and propaganda dissemination in Malaya.

The Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) monitors traffic volumes on its road network as part of its upkeep duties, utilizing a metric known as average annual daily traffic (AADT). This metric calculates the typical daily traffic flow over an entire year for a specific road section. In 2009, the department reported that the west segment of M-82, located west of Fremont, experienced the highest daily traffic with 16,532 vehicles, while the eastern segment near Newaygo witnessed the lowest traffic count at 4,018 vehicles per day. Moreover, the M-82 highway has not been included in the National Highway System, a critical infrastructure network vital for the nation's economic, defense, and transportation needs.

The contemporary M-82 traces its origins back to 1926, connecting at US 31 in Hart and terminating at the intersection of US 131 and M-46 in Howard City. This adjustment enabled the former Newaygo to Howard City portion to revert to the M-82 designation. The final modification occurred in 1978, when the overlap with M-120 was discontinued in favor of M-120. At this juncture, the M-82 designation was shortened to its western border at Fremont's junction, establishing the current highway route.

Meridian, located in Mississippi, USA, stands as the sixth most populous city within the state. Serving as the county seat for Lauderdale County, it also acts as the core component of the Meridian, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. Strategically positioned along key highways, Meridian is situated at a distance of 93 miles (150 kilometers) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 kilometers) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 kilometers) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; and 231 miles (372 kilometers) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Founded in 1860, Meridian's economic foundation was established at the crossroads of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and the Southern Railway of Mississippi. Initially, the city thrived due to its pivotal role in railway commerce and the transportation of various goods. Consequently, it evolved into a significant hub for trade transactions. Notably, during the American Civil War, the city suffered extensive damage when General William Tecumseh Sherman initiated a destructive campaign known as the Battle of Meridian, resulting in much of the urban area being set ablaze in February 1864.

Post-war reconstruction saw the city flourish into what was then the largest urban center in Mississippi from 1890 to 1930, and it became a pivotal hub for manufacturing in the Southern region, with an impressive daily train traffic of 44 arrivals and departures. The Union Station, constructed in 1906, has since evolved into a multi-modal transportation hub providing access to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways; an average of 242 to 360 passengers are served annually. Despite the economic downturn following the waning of the railroad industry, the city has adapted, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing being the primary employers as of 2010. Based on 2008 census projections, the city's population within its boundaries is estimated at 38,232. However, a significantly larger regional influence extends beyond these city limits, encompassing a population of around 232,900 within a 45-mile radius and an even broader demographic of approximately 526,500 within a 65-mile radius. Notably, around 104,600 and 234,200 of these residents are part of the active labor market, contributing substantially to the city's economy.

Two military establishments, Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, supply employment for more than 4,000 individuals in the region. NAS Meridian houses both the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and the initial Department of Homeland Security location in the state. Named in honor of brothers Fred and Al Key, who set a world record for endurance flight in 1935, Key Field now accommodates the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard along with a support center for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. Rush Foundation Hospital is the leading non-military employer in the area, with 2,610 employees on staff.

In addition to Meridian's various arts institutions and heritage sites, such as the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra, the city once housed two Carnegie libraries. One was designated exclusively for white residents, while the other catered to African American communities. Notably, the Carnegie Branch Library, which has since been demolished, was part of a series of public libraries constructed by the Carnegie Foundation for black populations in the segregated South of the United States.

Selected for the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center's (Mississippi Arts & Entertainment) future residence, the city boasts a rich history, including the birthplace of "Father of Country Music," Jimmie Rodgers. His legacy is commemorated at the Highland Park Museum, showcasing artifacts from his life and career, alongside vintage steam-era railway equipment. Another highlight is the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, recognized as a National Historic Landmark, being the globe's sole stationary two-row Dentzel menagerie. Among its notable residents are Miss America 1986, Susan Akin, James Chaney - a civil rights activist tragically murdered in 1964 during the Mississippi civil rights workers' attacks, and Hartley Peavey, founder of Peavey Electronics, a company with headquarters in Meridian. The city's historical significance continues with the federal courthouse; it served as the venue for the 1966-67 trial concerning the murder of Chaney and other activists, marking a pivotal moment where a white jury successfully convicted a white official for a civil rights violation.

Originally home to the Choctaw indigenous people, the region now known as Meridian was acquired by the United States through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek in 1830, a part of the broader era referred to as Indian Removal. Following the treaty's ratification, there was an influx of European-American pioneers who started settling in the territory.

Following the acquisition of a federal land grant spanning approximately 2,000 acres (810 hectares), Richard McLemore, the pioneer of Meridian, initiated the offering of free land to lure additional settlers into the area with the aim of fostering its growth and development. The vast majority of this land was purchased by Lewis A. Ragsdale, an attorney from Alabama, in 1853. John T. Ball, a businessman hailing from Kemper County, acquired the leftover 80 acres (0.32 square kilometers). Ragsdale and Ball, later recognized as the city's founders, proceeded to delineate plots for future urban expansion on their individual landholdings.

The naming dispute for the proposed settlement was intense, involving various factions advocating for different monikers. Ball, along with the industrious citizens, favored "Meridian," interpreting it as interchangeable with "junction"; meanwhile, the predominantly rural populace preferred "Unknown," derived from a local stream's native American moniker, symbolizing "mad river." Ragsdale proposed "Ragsdale City" as his choice. Ball constructed a station house on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, featuring a sign that alternated daily between "Meridian" and "Unknown." As the railroad industry expanded and attracted workers, their influence led to "Meridian" being permanently emblazoned on the station's signage. On February 10, 1860, the town was officially recognized as Meridian.

Meridian started off as a small settlement when the American Civil War erupted in 1861, occupying a critical location at a railway intersection that attracted significant military development by the Confederates to bolster their war efforts. In 1864, during the Battle of Meridian, General William Tecumseh Sherman orchestrated the entry of his troops into the town, causing widespread devastation through the destruction of railroads in all directions, an arsenal, and large stockpiles. His forces razed many buildings to the ground. Following the battle, Sherman reportedly declared, "Meridian, including its warehouses, supply depots, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and barracks, no longer exists." Despite the extensive destruction, the railroad infrastructure in the city was swiftly restored; within just 26 operational days after the conflict, the lines were back in service. This recovery marked a notable feat. The period of Reconstruction witnessed continued tension regarding race relations, exemplified by the 1871 riot that ensued after a fire damaging numerous local businesses.

Following the Civil War, the town flourished and entered its "Golden Age" spanning from 1880 to 1910, largely due to the establishment of railroads that facilitated transportation and spurred industrial growth, leading to a significant population increase. As the population surged, so did commercial activities within the downtown district. Between 1890 and 1930, Meridian became the largest city in Mississippi and a prominent hub for manufacturing in the Southern region. Numerous historic buildings within the city were constructed during or shortly after this period, such as the Grand Opera House in 1890, the Wechsler School in 1894, two Carnegie libraries in 1913, and the <unk> Building, known as the tallest skyscraper in Meridian by 1929.

The city experienced significant expansion due to the commission government's strategic initiative to attract 90 new industrial establishments in 1913, alongside the thriving automotive sector in the 1920s. Remarkably, the city managed to retain its momentum and allure for new businesses even during the economic turmoil of the 1929 stock market crash and the subsequent Great Depression. During the darkest years of the Depression, when people sought distractions and comfort, luxury became a desirable commodity for the masses. This shift in cultural preferences led to the construction of the S. H. Kress & Co. building, designed to "provide luxury to the common man," in downtown Meridian, along with the opening of the Temple Theater, which was repurposed into a movie house. The federal courthouse, a testament to public works, was erected in 1933 under the Works Progress Administration (WPA) program.

Following a short economic downturn near the conclusion of the Great Depression, the nation was engulfed by World War II, reigniting the significance of railroads. These infrastructures played a pivotal role in facilitating the transportation of essential resources like gasoline and scrap metal, which were crucial for manufacturing military equipment, thereby reestablishing Meridian as the regional rail hub. This period of renewed economic growth persisted until the 1950s when the automobile and the Interstate Highway System gained prominence over passenger rail services. The subsequent decline in the railroad sector led to substantial job losses, contributing to a population decrease as workers migrated to other regions in search of employment opportunities.

In the 1960s, during the American Civil Rights Movement, Meridian served as the hub for the Council of Federated Organizations' (COFO) operations and numerous other activist groups. The city was also the site where local activists, including James Chaney, alongside Michael Schwerner, his spouse Rita Schwerner Bender, and Andrew Goodman, who were volunteers from the North, worked diligently to establish a community center. This initiative aimed to empower African Americans in the region by conducting classes aimed at helping them reclaim their voting rights. The presence of these individuals inevitably fueled racial tensions within the area, often leading to outbreaks of violence. 

On June 21, 1964, Chaney, Schwerner, and Goodman ventured to Neshoba County, Mississippi, to meet with members of a black church that had recently suffered a bombing and arson attack. Tragically, the trio vanished that night as they returned towards Meridian. Subsequent to a comprehensive FBI investigation, their bodies were discovered two months later, buried beneath an earthen dam.

In a landmark case, seven Klansmen, one of whom was a deputy sheriff, were found guilty in the federal courthouse in Meridian for "denying individuals their civil liberties," while three others were acquitted in the Mississippi civil rights workers' murder trial. This was significant as it marked the first instance where a white jury convicted a white official for a civil rights-related killing. In 2005, the case was revisited by the state, which for the first time initiated charges against the perpetrators. Edgar Ray Killen was subsequently convicted for manslaughter and sentenced to serve sixty years in prison. Following this verdict, Meridian honored the memory of Michael Chaney by renaming part of 49th Avenue in his honor and establishing an annual memorial service to commemorate his life.

From the 1960s onward, as a result of the development of highways that facilitated commuting, people started relocating from the central business district towards newer residential areas situated to the north. In response to the establishment of strip commercial establishments within the downtown area, city authorities took steps in the 1970s and 1980s to designate several zones as historic districts with the objective of safeguarding the architectural identity of the city. This protective measure was further solidified through the creation of the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission in 1979, and the inception of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street carried out various initiatives aimed at rejuvenating the downtown area, notably constructing a new Amtrak station in 1997, which was modeled after a historic train station that once symbolized Meridian's prosperity but had since been dismantled. Additional endeavors encompassed the restoration of the Rosenbaum Building in 2001 and Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, alongside fostering a harmonious integration of urban planning. Together with The Riley Foundation, they embarked on the revitalization and conversion of the iconic Grand Opera House in 2006, transforming it into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

Following the transfer of the Meridian Main Street to the Alliance for Downtown Meridian in the latter part of 2007, these entities, along with the Meridian Downtown Association, initiated the drive for downtown rejuvenation. The Alliance operates as a consolidating entity, enabling the other organizations to leverage its staff and resources. Simultaneously, it facilitates communication among them. An endeavor to refurbish the <unk> Building was in progress until the newly elected Mayor, Cheri Barry, halted these plans at the beginning of 2010. Presently, the Alliance's role involves promoting additional growth and restoration within downtown. Its objective is to assist enterprises, particularly unique shops, eateries, and lounges, which contribute to heightened daytime and evening activity in the area. The Meridian Downtown Association's main objective is to increase pedestrian traffic downtown through organized events, while the Meridian Main Street program supports the ongoing businesses in the downtown area.

Meridian's role as a railway hub has significantly contributed to the establishment of numerous hotels. Prior to entering its "Golden Age," the city witnessed the construction of substantial hotels, such as the Great Southern and the Grand Avenue hotels, during the early part of the 20th century. The expansion of railroads and the inception of the initial Union Station in 1906 facilitated the building of accommodations for travelers and staff. In 1905, the Elmira Hotel came into existence, followed by the Terminal Hotel in 1910. The Hotel Meridian was erected in 1907, while the Union Hotel was constructed in 1908. Notably, the Union Hotel was recognized on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979. Both Hotel Meridian and the Grand Avenue Hotel were designated as integral components of the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

As the city expanded, the hotels mirrored the thriving economy, exemplified by the construction of the eleven-story skyscraper, the Lamar Hotel, in 1927. Recognized on the National Register of Historic Places since 1979, the Lamar Hotel underwent adaptation to serve as a county annex facility. In 1988, its historical significance was further acknowledged when it was designated as a Mississippi Landmark.

The E.F. Young Hotel, constructed in 1931, served as a pivotal fixture within an African-American business hub that emerged to the west of the city's central area. This establishment was one of the few accommodations available in the segregated era for itinerant African-Americans seeking lodging.

Following urban expansion into suburban areas during the 1960s and 70s, many hotels relocated outside of the central business district. The revitalization of the Riley Center in 2006 spurred an interest in a new downtown hotel, leading to the proposal of redeveloping the <unk> Building for this purpose. However, restoration efforts encountered setbacks due to changes in municipal leadership. Recognizing the need for community engagement and support for the building's renovation, the <unk> Preservation Society was established in 2013. Since its inception, the organization has organized tours of the first floor and hosted anniversary events aimed at raising public awareness and enthusiasm for preserving the site.

Meridian boasts nine areas recognized on the National Register of Historic Places, with its Meridian Downtown Historic District being a merge of the Meridian Urban Center Historic District and the Union Station Historic District. These districts showcase a diverse array of architectural styles prevalent during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, such as Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Italianate, Art Deco, Late Victorian, and Bungalow designs. Notably, the historic areas include:

1. **Meridian Downtown Historic District** - This area amalgamates the Meridian Urban Center Historic District and the Union Station Historic District.
2. **Meridian Urban Center Historic District**
3. **Union Station Historic District**
4. **Historic Downtown Meridian**
5. **East 6th Street**
6. **Lanier Street Historic District**
7. **Northeast Meridian**
8. **South Meridian**
9. **Westerly District**

All these sites are marked by architectural styles typical of their respective eras, reflecting the rich heritage and evolution of urban design in Meridian.

Meridian has been governed by a mayoral-council system, often referred to as a "strong mayor" format, since 1985. In this structure, the mayor is directly elected by the entire city population every four years. Comprised of five members, the city council is elected from each of the city's five wards, each treated as a distinct electoral district, every four years. The mayor, acting as the city's chief executive officer, oversees and directs the daily operations of municipal government. Meanwhile, the city council serves in a legislative capacity, establishing policies and annually approving the city's operating budget, thus functioning as the governing body's policymaking entity.

The City Hall, designated as a historic landmark on the National Register, is situated at 601 23rd Avenue. The incumbent mayor is Percy Bland. The city council's membership comprises Dr. George M. Thomas representing Ward 1, Kenneth Dustin Markham for Ward 2, Barbara Henson for Ward 3, Kim Houston for Ward 4, and Randy Hammon for Ward 5. Pam McInnis serves as the council clerk. Altogether, the municipality employs approximately 570 individuals.

Following Hurricane Katrina's devastation in 2005, the city promptly established the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), marking it as the sole local DHS entity within the state. This DHS organization is responsible for overseeing operations across nine counties. With a financial boost of $2.5 million in grants from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and other organizations, the department embarked on an initiative to train law enforcement officers from neighboring Southern states in passenger rail rescue techniques and also offered a range of civilian courses including basic handgun instruction, Boy Scout first aid, hunting basics, and comprehensive firearms training. 

The department played a crucial role during the 2005 hurricane season, notably assisting in managing shelters for 700 evacuees during Hurricane Ivan. The city's leadership in this DHS effort was further solidified as it led one of the task forces within the wider Mississippi DHS structure, which is composed of combined operations from three distinct nine-county teams.

Since 2009, under the leadership of Police Chief Lee, the Meridian Police Department comprises a total of 115 full-time officers along with part-time and reserve personnel. In 2009, their Criminal Investigations Division handled 4,000 cases, with 2,000 being classified as felonies. Reports for that year indicated a slight increase in offenses compared to the previous year. Meridian is often cited as the "safest city in Mississippi" with over 30,000 residents. Notably, the East Mississippi Correctional Facility, managed by the GEO Group on behalf of the Mississippi Department of Corrections, is situated in an unincorporated area of Lauderdale County, close to Meridian. 

As for the Meridian Fire Department, it's headed by Chief Anthony Clayton. In 2009, they addressed over 1,600 calls, encompassing 123 structural fires and 609 emergency services incidents.

In the realm of state governance, Mississippi's Senate district configuration segments the city into three primary zones. The northern extremity of the municipality is encompassed within the 31st State Senate District, with Senator Terry Clark Burton (Republican) holding office there. A linear stretch, starting from the southwestern boundary and stretching up to the northeastern edge of the city, forms part of the 32nd State Senate District, served by Sampson Jackson, II (Democrat). Meanwhile, the western and southeastern parts of the city are included in the 33rd State Senate District, currently led by Senator <unknown> Carmichael (Republican).

Regarding the Mississippi House of Representatives, the city is allocated into four distinct districts. The southern and eastern sections of the city are included in House District 81, represented by Steven A. Horne (Republican). The heart of the city constitutes House District 82 in its entirety, with Representative Wilbert L. Jones (Democrat) serving this area. Adjacent to House District 82 is House District 83, represented by Greg Snowden (Republican). Lastly, the western portion of the city, alongside a small northern segment, falls under House District 84, which is led by Tad Campbell (Republican).

At the national level, Meridian is situated within Mississippi's 3rd congressional district, which is currently served by Gregg Harper (a member of the Republican Party), having held the position since 2009. Lauderdale County, which includes Meridian, has consistently supported the Republican candidate in every United States presidential election since 1972. Before the county's political alignment with the Republicans, its white electorate predominantly voted for Democratic candidates. This pattern reflects Lauderdale County's historical status as a one-party state, a situation that persisted from the late 19th century onwards.

The demographic changes within the metropolis have been significantly influenced by a complex interplay of socio-economic dynamics. Since its establishment, the population witnessed a continuous rise during each decennial census, albeit with fluctuating growth percentages that ranged from an astonishing 165% to an exceptionally low 0.2%. The scenario took a dramatic turn in the 1970s, marking a notable decrease in population count; however, it experienced a slight recovery by the 1980s. The trend then shifted into a prolonged phase of decline, which only started reversing around the dawn of the 21st century. Specifically, between 1980 and 2000, there was a substantial decrease of over 14% in the population size. By the time of the 2000 census, the city's resident count was recorded at 39,968 individuals, with a population density of approximately 885.9 inhabitants per square kilometer (342.0 inhabitants per square mile). In 2008, it stood as the sixth-largest municipality in the state. As of 2010, there was a notable increase in the populace, reflecting the ongoing evolution of the city's demographic landscape.

Meridian serves as the leading municipality within the Meridian metropolitan region, an area encompassing the three counties of Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale since 2009, with a total population recorded at approximately 106,139 inhabitants. This region exhibits a significant population density expanding up to 232,900 individuals within a 45-mile radius. Moreover, extending further out to a 65-mile radius, the population density escalates to around 526,500 people.

Despite fluctuations in the city's total population, there has been a consistent rise in both the count and the proportion of non-white inhabitants. The lone exception to this trend occurred between 1960 and 1970, coinciding with a significant decrease in the city's overall population. According to the 2010 Census, the demographic structure of the city was as follows: 61.55% were African American, 35.71% were Caucasian, 0.9% were Asian, 0.2% were Native American, less than 0.02% were Pacific Islander, 0.59% belonged to other racial groups, and 0.89% identified with multiple races. The Hispanic or Latino community comprised 1.75% of the total population.

Based on the 2000 Census, within the city's boundaries, there were 17,890 housing units, out of which 15,966 were inhabited at that time. Of these occupied units, 10,033 housed families. Statistics indicate that 31.1% of the occupied households contained children under 18, whereas 36.2% comprised married couples residing together. A segment of 23.3% consisted of single-female households without husbands present, while 37.2% were categorized as non-family units. It is noted that 33.2% of all households consisted of individuals, and 14.0% included someone over the age of 65 living alone. The average household size stood at 2.39 people, and the typical family size was 3.06 members.

The average household size has shown a consistent decline since 1970, when it was recorded at 3.04 people. Meridian's median age experienced an increase from 30.4 years in 1970 to 34.6 years in 2000.

The median household income in the city stood at $25,085, whereas the median income for families amounted to $31,062. Male residents demonstrated a higher median income at $29,404, compared to $19,702 for females. The average personal income within the city was reported as $15,255. Approximately 24.6% of families, along with 28.6% of the total population, were classified as living in poverty. This situation disproportionately affected younger individuals, with 40.8% of those under 18 years old in poverty, and older individuals, where 22.0% of those aged 65 and above fell below the poverty threshold.

In Meridian, the proportion of people who are religiously affiliated is notably higher than the national average, with approximately 65.2% of Lauderdale County's populace associating themselves with religious congregations, in contrast to the national average of 50.2%. In the year 2000, the demographic breakdown revealed that 30,068 individuals, or roughly 59.0%, were part of the Southern Baptist Convention, 9,469 made up around 18.6% as members of the United Methodist Church, and 1,872 accounted for about 3.7% affiliated with the Catholic Church.

Jewish immigrants from Germany and Eastern Europe played a significant role in Meridian's commercial expansion, establishing businesses and services. Congregation Beth Israel was established in 1868, preceding the city's "Golden Age." Historically, Meridian was home to the state's largest Jewish population, numbering around 575 individuals in 1927. However, the contemporary Jewish community is notably smaller, with less than 40 Jews currently residing in the city, with the majority being seniors.

Meridian, situated within the North Central Hills region of Mississippi in Lauderdale County, was delineated by the United States Census Bureau as having a total surface area of 45.9 square miles (119 km²), comprising 45.1 square miles (117 km²) of land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 km²) of water. Distances from major thoroughfares reveal that the city is 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 km) west of Atlanta, Georgia. The surrounding area is marked by expanses of cotton and corn fields intertwined with oak and pine forests, with a landscape characterized by clay hills and the initial stretches of the <unk> River's tributaries.

The urban core of the city has undergone transformation, with modifications to the natural terrain through processes like leveling. However, the region retains a soothing undulating feature in the outskirts. The city is dotted with numerous small creeks that flow throughout it, and there are small lakes and woodland areas located in both the northern and southern sections. Specifically, a creek traverses the southern part of the city, subsequently dividing into Gallagher's Creek, which meanders through the city's central area. Elsewhere, in the western extremities of the city, Loper's Creek flows while there are smaller streams scattered across the city territory, such as Shearer's Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek.

Based in the humid subtropical climate region, Meridian experiences typical seasonal variations. During the summer months (June to August), the mean daily high temperatures usually hover around 90°F (32°C), with nightly lows averaging approximately 70°F (21°C). In contrast, during the winter period from December to February, the mean daytime temperatures typically reach around 60°F (16°C) while nighttime temperatures dip to about 35°F (2°C). July represents the warmest month with an average peak temperature of 92.9°F (33.3°C), whereas January is the coldest month, featuring an average low temperature of 34.3°F (1.5°C).

The city experiences an annual precipitation average of 58-65 inches (1,490 mm), with rainfall distribution being relatively uniform throughout the year. March emerges as the wettest month, typically witnessing approximately 6.93 inches (176 mm) of precipitation. Thunderstorms contribute significantly to rainfall, especially during summer months but are prevalent all year round. Such storms might result in severe conditions including damaging winds, substantial hail, alongside standard perils like lightning and heavy rains, sometimes leading to destructive events. These extreme thunderstorms are most frequent during spring, with another significant occurrence noted during the fall season. Additionally, these storms increase the likelihood of tornado outbreaks.

In the beginning, the local economy relied heavily on the extensive railway network present in the area. As the largest city in Mississippi during the early 1900s, it boasted five significant rail routes and experienced a daily flow of 44 trains carrying a variety of goods. The city's prosperity was intertwined with both the rail system and the commodities transported via it, notably timber and cotton. During the period roughly spanning from 1890 to 1930, the city became a significant economic powerhouse within the state and broader region due to its thriving railway-based industries.

Despite facing economic downturns following the waning fortunes of the railroading sector in the 1950s, the city has shown resilience and adaptability. It transitioned away from an economy primarily anchored in railway operations to a more diverse economic structure. Today, healthcare, defense-related sectors, and manufacturing are among the largest employers in the city, reflecting this evolution in its economic landscape.

Meridian, along with Lauderdale County and the city of Marion, is supported by the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, established in 1996 by a coalition of local business leaders. As of April 2010, the city's civilian workforce numbered at approximately 15,420 individuals. However, the demographic footprint extends significantly beyond these city limits: a 45-mile radius encompasses a population of roughly 232,900, while a 65-mile radius captures around 526,500 residents, out of which about 104,600 and 234,200, respectively, are part of the labor force. This makes Meridian a central node for employment, retail, healthcare, and cultural activities. Notably, 80% of Lauderdale County's workforce resides within the county itself, while 90% of this workforce lives within a 45-mile radius of the city center.

In April 2010, healthcare employment in Lauderdale County numbered 6,260 individuals. The top employer in the region was Rush Hospital, which had 2,610 staff members, surpassing East Mississippi State Hospital's 1,500 and Anderson Hospital's 1,475. Meridian hosts three hospitals and numerous additional healthcare institutions. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center specializes in cardiovascular surgery, featuring a level II newborn ICU and a health and fitness facility. Rush Foundation Hospital, part of the broader Rush Health Systems, runs the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, catering to long-term care for non-permanent patients needing extended hospital recovery. Riley Hospital offers two centers dedicated to stroke treatment and rehabilitation. Additional healthcare providers in Meridian include the Alliance Health Center and East Mississippi State Hospital, which has operated since 1882.

The retail sector significantly contributes to employment within the region, with approximately 5,280 individuals engaged in retail activities as of April 2010. Retail expenditure in the city amounts to nearly $2 billion annually. The expansive Bonita Lakes Mall, covering 633,685 square feet (58,871 m²), provides shoppers access to more than a hundred retail outlets. This includes a variety of establishments such as department stores, specialty shops, dining options, eateries, and an entertainment hub featuring United Artists Theatres. In November 2007, the first phase of construction for Meridian Crossroads—a sizable 375,000 square foot (34,800 m²) shopping center in the Bonita Lakes area—was successfully completed, thereby revitalizing the local retail landscape. Moreover, the North Hills Street retail area has witnessed steady growth, culminating in the opening of new retail and office spaces close to the Highway 19 Walmart Supercenter in March 2007.

The region is supported by two significant military establishments - Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field. These facilities together contribute more than 4,000 employment opportunities for the community. NAS Meridian specializes in providing training for naval carrier pilots along with other enlisted personnel. Additionally, it houses the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy, which offers narcotics training to law enforcement professionals across numerous southeastern states. Being home to the first Department of Homeland Security in the state, the city leads a nine-county regional response team and a twenty-nine county regional response task force. 

Key Field is historically notable as it was the stage for the 1935 world endurance flight record set by brothers Fred and Al Key. Presently, Key Field is the location for the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and a support facility for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. The area also features an exhibit documenting the evolution of aviation, which is part of Meridian's Aviation Museum.

As of April 2010, Lauderdale County's total manufacturing workforce amounted to 28,500 individuals. Peavey Electronics Corporation, founded in 1965, produces guitars, amplifiers, and audio systems, maintaining its principal office within the city's boundaries. Additional industries present in the region encompass Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, along with an unspecified corporation. The city further hosts four industrial estates.

The MSU Riley Center, situated in the heart of downtown, serves as a significant source of income through the promotion of tourism, artistic events, and entertainment sales. It draws over 60,000 individuals each year to downtown Meridian for various conferences, meetings, and shows. Loeb's Department Store, located on Front Street, continues to be a notable Mississippi retail icon, having been passed down through four generations of family ownership. The store has been in operation since 1887, originally founded by Alex Loeb, offering high-quality attire for both men and women.

Renowned for its artistic heritage spanning over a century, Meridian boasts numerous art and cultural organizations that organize various cultural gatherings. The closure of the Carnegie library on 25th Ave and 7th St led the Art Association to renovate it into the Meridian Museum of Art, establishing a dedicated space for exhibitions. This museum was inaugurated in 1970 and has continued to showcase revolving exhibitions alongside numerous educational activities catering to students and adults alike. Approximately thirty exhibitions are staged every year, encompassing a wide array of disciplines, including traditional decorative arts, ethnographic and tribal artifacts, photography, crafts, and various forms of artwork. The museum's collection also features 18th and 19th century portraits, 20th century photography, and several sculptures.

In 2000, a substantial $10 million grant from the Riley Foundation—a local organization established in 1998—initiated the restoration of the building. This initiative was supported by additional funding sourced through a combination of city, county, and federal grants amounting to $15 million.

This modernized facility features a 950-seat auditorium for live performances, a 200-seat studio theater, and boasts a total of 30,000 square feet (approximately 2,787 square meters) of versatile meeting spaces. The Riley Center has significantly contributed to the rejuvenation of downtown Meridian, attracting over 60,000 annual visitors for events including conferences, meetings, and theatrical performances.

Meridian Regional Airport, situated at Key Field on Airport Boulevard South, is conveniently positioned 3 miles (4.8 km) south-west of the city center. Notably, the airport boasts the state's longest public runway, measuring 10,004 feet (3,049 m). Originally operational since 1930, this facility provides daily flights connecting Meridian to Dallas/Fort Worth, Texas.

During the Great Depression, the city's inhabitants seriously considered discontinuing the airport due to the escalating costs of upkeep. However, in 1935, Fred and Al Key, the airport's managers and siblings, devised a strategy to sustain its operations. From June 4th to July 1st, they flew their aircraft, "Ole Miss," over the city. Their record-breaking flight for 27 days, totaling 653 hours and 34 minutes, garnered significant public attention and financial support for the city, ensuring the airport's continuity. As a tribute to their achievement, which stands as an unbroken record in conventional flight, the airport was renamed Key Field, in honor of the brothers.

The foundation of Meridian's early public education system was laid by the 1870 Mississippi Constitution. During the period from 1870 to 1885, boards of education, whose members were appointed by the City Council, governed the schools. Prior to 1884, there were multiple privately owned schools in the city with an enrollment of around 400 pupils. It wasn't until September 1884 that the city constructed its first public school facility. The city's first educational institution serving black students operated within buildings leased from St. Paul Methodist Church. The Mississippi Legislature recognized the city's autonomy in maintaining its own municipal school district by amending the city charter in January 1888. This legislative action led to the approval of $30,000 in bonds for the construction of new public schools in March of the same year. One of the outcomes of these bonds was the establishment of the Wechsler School in 1894, marking the inaugural brick public school building dedicated to African American students in the region.

Initially established as the Meridian Public School District, it has since expanded to encompass a total of six elementary schools, three middle schools, and three high schools. In addition to these public institutions, the city boasts several private educational options such as Lamar School, Calvary Christian School, Community Christian School, and St. Patrick's Catholic School. Meridian High School, serving as the central high school within the district, spans over 37 acres (15 hectares), featuring an array of six buildings and accommodating 111 classrooms. This high school, which accommodates grades ten through twelve, currently enrolls around 1,500 students.

Meridian is the setting for two institutions focused on post-secondary education. Established in 1937, Meridian Community College, which was initially named Meridian Junior College and situated within Meridian High School, relocated to its current location in 1965. Post the implementation of desegregation policies, the institution united with T.J. Harris Junior College in 1970, which earlier admitted African-American students. This amalgamation led to the renaming of Meridian Junior College to Meridian Community College in 1987, emphasizing its broadened scope in catering to the diverse needs of the expanding community. Additionally, Mississippi State University maintains a campus in Meridian. According to data from the Fall 2008 term, 763 students from 33 counties in Mississippi and some from Alabama were enrolled at this college.

Papa Stour is an island within the Shetland archipelago off the coast of Scotland, currently inhabited by fewer than twenty individuals. A notable influx of residents occurred during the 1970s as part of an initiative to populate the island. Geographically, Papa Stour spans 828 hectares or approximately 3.2 square miles, ranking it as the eighth-largest Shetland Island. The marine environment, particularly due to erosion shaping the soft volcanic rocks by the sea, has resulted in a remarkable array of geological features including caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, and cliffs. 

The island supports a rich tapestry of wildlife, making it a focal point for conservation efforts. Specifically, the western coastline has been designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, acknowledging its ecological significance. Furthermore, the waters surrounding Papa Stour are recognized as a Special Area of Conservation, emphasizing the importance of protecting its unique aquatic habitats and marine life.

This island boasts a collection of Neolithic burial chambers, alongside remnants of Duke Hakon's thirteenth-century dwelling, indicative of its Norse heritage on the premises. In the 19th century, the populace peaked at approximately 380 individuals, a period marked by the establishment of a fishing outpost in West Voe. Following this, there was a continuous drop in inhabitants until the figure dipped to an all-time low of just 16 in the 1970s; however, recent trends show a notable increase in population.

Located at the southwestern extremity of St Magnus Bay, Papa Stour features 34 kilometers (21 miles) of rugged shoreline characterized by numerous small coves and four larger voes. The most sheltered anchorage, known as The Voe, is situated in the southernmost part, with dramatic cliffs that house a natural rock arch. To the east lies Voe (Old Norse for 'harbour bay'), though somewhat less secluded, it serves as the primary port for the island and is the departure point for ferries.

Holm and Maiden Stack protect the harbor's southern entryway. Holm Island, which is a tidal island, was once a leper colony up until the eighteenth century; it's theorized that many inhabitants suffered from vitamin deficiencies, not leprosy. The name of Maiden Stack stems from a tale dating back to the fourteenth century. Allegedly, Lord Thorvald built a tiny dwelling atop the stack as a means to "preserve" his daughter from males. However, his plans didn't unfold as he intended because she was discovered to be pregnant upon her departure; alternatively, the story ends with her and her fisherman lover successfully escaping together. West Voe, whose inner section is known as 'unknown', is the principal bay on the northern coast, with a smaller bay, Voe, situated immediately to its west.

Today, the principal settlement on the island is situated at a location overlooking Unnamed Voe and is encircled by pasture land to the east of the hill dyke, which extends southward from West Voe. In contrast, the western section of the island is divided by a strip of glacial moraine stretching roughly 1.5 kilometers in length. The remainder of the terrain is characterized by a thin, stony soil often sourced from glacial debris. Peat is notably scarce across the island, and given the volcanic substratum, the soils tend to be fairly rich in nutrients. The absence of peat resulted in the practice of 'turf scalping' for fuel, leaving exposed patches of rock within the island's interior.

Apart from the larger islets previously mentioned, there are numerous smaller isles and skerries scattered along the coast of Papa Stour. Some notable ones are: the Unnamed Stack, Unnamed Skerry, Unnamed Skerry, Unnamed Skerry, Unnamed Holm, Unnamed Stacks, Melby's Holm, Koda Skerry, Lyra Skerry, unnamed Skerries, Skerry of unknown name, Sula Stack, Swat Skerry, The Horn, Unnamed Skerry, and Wilma Skerry. The Ve Skerries, which are located approximately 5 kilometers (around 3 miles) to the northwest, consist of: Unnamed, North Skerry, Unnamed, Unnamed, and The Clubb. The shallow seabed known as Papa @-@ <unk> is situated between Papa Stour and the Ve Skerries.

On June 21, 2008, Stuart Hill, the solitary inhabitant of the 1-hectare (2.5-acre) island referred to as "Unknown Holm," renamed it as "The Unknown Island" and made a proclamation of sovereignty, leading to the establishment of a Crown Dependency under his ownership. Relying on a matrimonial pact from 1468 between King Christian of Norway and King James III of Scotland, Hill contended that this should classify the island as a British Crown Dependency, positioning it outside the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom and the European Union. Despite this assertion, the United Kingdom did not validate this claim.

The Scottish island's geology is characterized by a blend of both volcanic and sedimentary rock types from the Devonian era. During this time, when the Scottish landmass was part of the Old Red Sandstone Continent, it was situated approximately 10 to 25 degrees south of the equator. The formation of the Old Red Sandstone sediments, which were laid down between 408 and 370 million years ago, resulted from the erosion of older Silurian rocks after they had been uplifted due to the process of Pangaea's formation. The now-deposited sediments were subsequently laid out in river delta formations. Freshwater Lake Orcadie was established near the margins of the eroding mountain range, stretching from Shetland to the southern part of the Moray Firth. The Papay Stour structure primarily consists of volcanic ash and lava deposits, stemming from this particular period, such as layers of hardened volcanic ash and lava (specifically rhyolite). Additionally, the region contains a Devonian fish fossil bed at Lamba Banks. These geological features are complemented by numerous large boulders, which were transported by glacial movements during the Pleistocene epoch.

The erosion of soft volcanic rocks by the sea has produced a remarkable assortment of geological formations, including caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, cliffs, voes, and unknown features, all considered among the most outstanding in Britain. A notable example is the 'Holloway', a cave traversing the northern-western extremity of the island, stretching nearly half a mile in length with sufficient width for rowing through. In the southwestern region, 'Christie's' (or alternatively named) Hole stands out as another magnificent cave, where part of its ceiling collapsed in 1981.
