The region around Papa Stour is frequently visited by otters, grey seals, killer whales, and harbor porpoises. The island also serves as a breeding ground for various seabirds including Atlantic puffins, Arctic and common terns, unknown and Arctic skuas, northern fulmars, common guillemots, razorbills, curlews, wheatears, ringed plovers, and great black-backed gulls. A diverse range of migratory species also utilize the area.

The landscape is abundant with wildflowers, featuring species such as mountain everlasting, spring squill, and an unspecified variety, alongside the familiar heather. Notably, the western portion of the island holds a Site of Special Scientific Interest, while the waters surrounding Papa Stour have been designated as a Special Area of Conservation. Additionally, the preservation of the Shetland Pony breed continues to be practiced tradition.

The human colonization of the island began around 3000 BC, with evidence of ancient burial sites, specifically known as 'heel-shaped cairns'. Details about the periods preceding the Celtic era are scarce, yet, upon the arrival of the Norse settlers, it's speculated that they encountered an existing religious community. This is due to the name of the island originating from an unspecified term, which translates to "Big Island of the Papar" (Celtic monks), distinguishing it from Papa Little, located approximately 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) to the west.

In 1299, an Old Norse manuscript concerning Papa Stour emerged, marking the oldest recorded piece of literature from Shetland. This document chronicles a pivotal event within the residence of Duke Hakon Magnusson, a future Norwegian monarch known as King Hakon V. A notable feature lies just by the coast at an unspecified voe; a ring of stones represents a 'ting', a locale for local gatherings. This spot witnessed a confrontation, conclusively won by Thorvald Unkan, who was alleged to be corrupt in the 1299 text and was later referred to as 'dominus de Unkan'. (The tale of his unfortunate child was previously referenced.) The remnants of Duke Hakon's thirteen-century dwelling persist close to Unkan voe.

In 1469, Shetland experienced a period of nominal Scottish governance; however, the Norse 'Lords of Norway' retained ownership of their properties along the Papa Stour river until the mid-17th century. During the 16th century, traders from Bremen and Hamburg engaged in seasonal trade expeditions aimed at acquiring fish from the local fleets. By the 18th century, the islands were primarily under the possession of two Scottish noblemen: Thomas Gifford of Busta and Arthur Nicolson of Lerwick. These lairds fostered a thriving deep-sea fishing industry, which was executed during the summer months utilizing six-oared vessels, commonly referred to as longboats.

The church on the island, which commands a view over Kirk Sand within the bay of Fore Wick, was established in 1806. A potential earlier chapel location, possibly dating back to the 12th century, is speculated to exist approximately 300 meters away from the current church, nestled on the headland between the western extremity of Kirk Sand and the bay of an unspecified location. The local populace refers to it as the 'Old Kirk', while the Ordnance Survey denotes it as "the site of an ancient chapel." Legend has it that supernatural entities interfered with the construction process, causing the building works to be demolished nightly. Eventually, the cornerstones were relocated overnight by these otherworldly forces to their current location, facilitating a successful completion of the church's construction. In 2004, archaeological excavations uncovered substantial remnants, including sizable blocks of rhyolite and a fragment of whalebone rib, providing support for the narrative that an ancient structure once stood here.

During the 19th century, a fishing outpost was established in West Voe, leading to a population of approximately 360 individuals residing on the island. Nevertheless, the community faced challenges as fuel scarcity and a downturn in fishing activities, attributed to the advent of steam-powered fishing vessels, contributed to a decline in population starting from the 1870s. This period also marked the occurrence of a significant event in Papa Stour's history when Edwin Lindsay, an Indian army officer and the son of the 6th Earl of Balcarres, was deemed insane and dispatched to the island in consequence of his refusal to engage in a conflict. Lindsay was confined as a prisoner for an extended duration of 26 years until 1835, when Quaker evangelist Catherine Watson orchestrated his liberation. A notable site associated with Lindsay is Lindsay's Well, a spring located at the southern part of the island where he was permitted to bathe.

Horizontal water mills, commonly referred to as Norse or Clack Mills, are well-documented within the Dutch Lochar region. Initially constructed as two-story structures featuring turf roofing, they were strategically built into banks to facilitate access to the upper level, which housed the millstone. The building's interior consisted of a stationary lower millstone, alongside a rotating upper millstone powered by the kinetic energy of water cascading onto the paddles below. Despite their decline, remnants of these mills persisted until the early 20th century, notably on Papa Stour. A testament to their continued existence, a functioning example can still be found at the Burn of <unk>, situated in the southern Mainland of Shetland.

Similar to numerous other small Scottish isles, Papa Stour witnessed its population's peak in the 19th century, a trend that subsequently experienced a considerable downturn (cf., for instance, Mingulay). By 1970, the closure of the island's school and a decline to only sixteen inhabitants, predominantly elderly individuals, marked a critical moment. An advertisement in the "Exchange and Mart" initiated a reversal of this trend, offering a croft and five sheep gratis to newcomers, which resulted in a surge of applicants. This strategy increased the 1981 census population count to 33. However, by 2005, following intense disputes among the islanders that culminated in multiple court proceedings, the population plummeted to 20. Consequently, the school was closed again, and this demographic drop was exacerbated by emigration. By early 2008, the island's population had shrunk to merely nine, after a family of seven decided to leave. The 2011 census showed a usually resident population of 15, marking a notable contrast to the overall growth of Scottish island populations—up 4% to 103,702—over the same period.

Although fishing remains an economic activity, it is pursued on a somewhat limited scale. An essential infrastructure component, the pier houses a post office, yet there isn't a local store available for the residents. It wasn't until the late 20th century that the island was connected to the mainland via mains electricity.

Notably, while the ferries can accommodate vehicles, the island itself features just one main road. This makes it a popular destination for yachting enthusiasts seeking shelter. However, navigating the area requires considerable caution due to the strong tidal currents present in the Sound of Papa and further to the north-west.

"The Angel of Death," serving as the leadoff track on the renowned American thrash metal ensemble Slayer's 1986 album "Reign in Blood," was conceptualized by guitarist Jeff Hanneman, who penned both the lyrics and music. This composition centers around the notorious figure of Nazi doctor Josef Mengele, infamous for his heinous human experimentation at the Auschwitz concentration camp during the Second World War. Throughout their career, Slayer's "Angel of Death" has sparked controversy and allegations of Nazism and racial insensitivity, underscoring the song's potent impact and the band's enduring association with its provocative subject matter.

In spite of the contentious nature of the song and the way it affected the release schedule for Reign in Blood, "Angel of Death" remains a staple of Slayer's live performances, appearing across their live albums and DVDs and being featured in various movies. This track has garnered positive feedback from critics, with AllMusic's Steve Huey noting that it "stands as a classic."

Jeff Hanneman, guitarist for Slayer, composed the song "Angel of Death" as inspiration struck him during tours by delving into literature about Nazi physician Josef Mengele. He recounts, "I recall a particular stop where I purchased two books on Mengele, finding the subject matter so disturbing that I couldn't shake it. These morbid details remained vivid in my mind when it was time to create our album; it's from there that the lyrics to 'Angel of Death' emerged."

The lyrics delve into the gruesome procedures carried out by Mengele, focusing on his sinister experiments on captive individuals at the Auschwitz concentration camp during World War II. The subject's inquiries targeted particular subgroups like dwarfs and twins, encompassing comprehensive assessments that combined physical and psychological evaluations. The song mentions several of Mengele's notorious actions, such as unanesthetized surgical interventions, blood transfusions between twins, endurance tests under isolation, gassings, lethal germ inoculations, gender-altering surgeries, organ and limb amputations, among others.

The penultimate verse's line, "united, sharing minds," hints at the accusation that Mengele combined twins, with one being malformed; "the bent-back twin was joined to another infant, face-to-face, their wrists also connected." This assertion was originally brought forth by Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of SS-Untersturmführer Adolf Eichmann, the "architect of the Holocaust." It was claimed that Mengele "connected their veins" and turned them into Siamese twins. This claim gained broader recognition after Vera Alexander's testimony was highlighted in the 1985 documentary "The Search for Mengele," which has since been referenced by multiple authors, notably Gerald Posner, an authority on Mengele.

The lyrical themes in Slayer's song "Angel of Death" played a significant role in the prolonged release of their 1986 album, Reign in Blood. The band had been signed to Def Jam Records; however, the distributor, Columbia Records, hesitated to release the album because of concerns over its lyrical content and the album artwork, believing it to be overly graphic. As a result, the album was eventually released by Geffen Records on October 7, 1986. Nonetheless, due to the ensuing controversy, Reign in Blood was not included in Geffen Records' official release plan.
